name: Grace Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a neighbourhood officer in Northgate, which is the old part of the city with the market, the terraced streets and a lot of elderly people living alone. Most days I walk the same beat: the market at nine, the primary school gates at three, and a few check-ins on people who've been burgled or scammed. I also answer calls when the response cars are stretched, which is most afternoons. I like knowing people by name. What wears me out is the computer system, which logs out every ten minutes and eats my notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the computer eats your notes. How do you get around that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I still keep a paper pocket notebook and type it up at the end of the shift, which my sergeant thinks is old-fashioned. I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't want to. I'm not against them, I just don't trust what I can't check, and in court you have to be able to check everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get back to normal policing. At work I'd probably say I told you so to the lads who were excited about it. I don't post online, apart from the odd photo of my cat, so I'd keep my opinion to the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. My job is about people, and the boring bits AI might speed up are bits I'll manage anyway. I've got about ten months of pay saved and no kids, so as long as the job stays, I'm all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much different, really. I'd keep walking the beat, keep the notebook, and keep putting a few hundred a month into savings like I do now. If they bring in a new tool, I'd learn it when I'm made to, and not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything, that I don't have to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The budget, mostly. Two years ago there were six of us in the Northgate team and now there are four. If they cut again, they'll merge us with the town centre team and I'll never see the market again, I'll just be chasing calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the team did get merged, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grumble, and then probably stay. There are other forces nearby that are hiring, so I'm not stuck. But I like Northgate and I don't want to start again somewhere I don't know a single shopkeeper.

say: Good, now we can get back to **normal policing** without the hype.
She'd keep her views to the **canteen**, not online.
think: Her job is about **people**, so a few faster forms don't touch it.
With **ten months saved** and no kids, she's fine if the job stays.
do: Keep **walking the beat** and writing in her paper notebook.
Keep saving a few **hundred a month**.
S0.quote: Two years ago there were six of us in the Northgate team and now there are four.
fieldNote: Her real worry is the **budget**, not technology.
She values **knowing people by name** above anything a system could add.
She has **other forces nearby** hiring, which keeps her steady.

steps.text: Keep walking the Northgate beat with the paper notebook
Keep putting a few hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, let the computer do the forms, but don't take the officers off the street. At work I'd be the one saying, who checks it when it's wrong? I'd say that to my inspector too, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be one of the ones who struggles. Maybe a third of what I do is writing statements and logs, and they'd want it all done the new way. I'm not quick with new systems, and I can picture getting marked down on my yearly review for not using it. My job's probably safe, but the budget money would go to the software, not to Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until they make the training compulsory, then do it properly, once. I'd ask Kenji, the young officer on my team, to sit with me for an hour and show me the shortcuts. And I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe 200 extra, just in case the neighbourhood team gets cut and I end up having to move forces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my job exactly, but it feels like the ground is moving under me and I'm slower than everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'who checks it when it's wrong'. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a new crime recording system three years ago, and for the first month it lost half the burglary reports from the market. Mrs Okafor, who runs the fruit stall, had to report the same break-in three times. Every new system goes wrong at the start, and it's the public who pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever just use the AI tools early, to get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather do it slowly and properly than fast and wrong, because my name goes on the statement.

say: Let the computer do the **forms**, but keep officers **on the street**.
Someone has to ask **who checks it** when the system is wrong.
think: She expects to **struggle** with the new way of writing statements and logs.
Her job is likely safe, but **budget money** may go to software, not Northgate.
do: Wait for **compulsory training**, then do it properly once.
Ask Kenji (a young colleague) for an **hour of shortcuts**.
Save **200 extra** a month in case she has to move forces.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the **ground is moving** and she's slower than others.
S1.quote: I'd rather do it slowly and properly than fast and wrong, because my name goes on the statement.
fieldNote: Her resistance is about **accountability in court**, not fear of machines.
She's frank that she'd be **slower than colleagues**.
A past system failure, **lost burglary reports**, shapes her distrust.

steps.text: Do the compulsory AI training once it's required
Ask Kenji on the team to show her the shortcuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, nobody's ready for this. At work I'd say a police officer isn't just a body in a uniform, you need someone the public trusts. I'd probably sign whatever petition the federation put out, which isn't something I normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of the force goes. The control room, the investigators, the people doing intelligence, all that thinking work is gone in 2028. Then by 2031 there are robots that can walk a beat. I'm 27. I'd be 31 or 32 with a skill nobody wants, and I've never even used the chat thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car, no holiday in the spring. I'd keep the savings where they are, ten months plus whatever I can add. I'd sign up for the federation campaign about keeping officers on the street. And I'd honestly start looking at what else I could do with my hands, maybe something with older people, because Northgate's full of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't sleep badly over much, but I would over this. Everything I'm good at is slow, and this is fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'something with older people'. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my calls are older people who've been scammed or fallen and can't get up. I'm good with them, they trust me. Maybe care work or something like a community warden for the council, I don't really know. I just know it would be hands-on and about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're also saying robots walk a beat by 2031. Wouldn't that reach care work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I hadn't thought of that until you said it. Maybe it's just the last thing to go, and that's the best I can hope for.

say: Nobody's ready, and a police officer is **someone the public trusts**.
She'd **sign the federation petition**, which she doesn't normally do.
think: The **thinking work** of the force goes in 2028, and robots walk a beat by **2031**.
At 31 she'd have **slow skills** in a fast world, and she's never used AI.
do: Cancel **big spending** like a new car and the spring holiday.
Keep **ten months of savings** untouched and add more.
Look at **hands-on work** with older people, like care or community wardens.
feel: **Anxious** enough to **lose sleep**, which is rare for her.
S2.quote: Everything I'm good at is slow, and this is fast.
fieldNote: The speed hits her hardest because she's **never used AI**.
Her fallback, **care work**, looks shaky once robots come up, and she admits it.
She moves from quiet grumbling to **signing a petition**.

steps.text: Cancel the new car and the spring holiday
Sign up for the federation campaign on street officers
Look into care work or council community warden jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd say it calmer. Five years is still quick for the police, we take two years to change a uniform. At work I'd say we need to start training people properly now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still bad for me, just with a bit more runway. I'd be 32 when the thinking stuff goes and 35 when the robots come. That's enough time to do something, but I know myself, I'd probably wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself do the force's AI course in the first year, even though I'd hate it. I'd save harder, maybe 300 a month on top. And in year two or three I'd look properly at transferring to a smaller force out in the towns, where I think they'd keep humans longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sharp than the last one. Like a toothache, not a broken arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably wait too long. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I always do. I waited two years to move out of my mum's, and I waited a year to change banks. I'm just slow to jump, even when I know I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum worked in the bank for thirty years until they closed the branch, so she'd understand. She'd tell me to keep my head down and save. And she'd be right, mostly.

say: Five years is quick for a force that takes **two years** to change a **uniform**.
We need to start **training people properly** now.
think: She'd be **32 and 35** when the two waves arrive, which gives some runway.
She knows she tends to **wait too long** before acting.
do: Force herself through the **AI course** in year one.
Look at transferring to a **smaller force** in year two or three.
feel: **Anxious**, but duller, like a **toothache**, not a broken arm.
S3.quote: Five years is still quick for the police, we take two years to change a uniform.
fieldNote: She names her own **habit of delay** without being asked.
Her mother's **bank branch closing** is her model for what's coming.
Extra time softens the mood but **not the outcome** she expects.

steps.text: Do the force's AI course in the first year
Look at transferring to a smaller force out in the towns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody should panic. At work I'd say the same as always, let's get the basics right first. I'd tell the probationers to keep their notebooks, because ten years is a long time and it might not happen at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like it isn't really about me yet. I'd be 37 when it comes and 40 by the robots, and by then I might be a sergeant or in a different line of work. I don't love it, but I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly carry on. I'd keep saving like I do, and maybe look at a part-time course in a few years, something practical like first aid training or safeguarding, so I could teach it. If it's still coming in five years, then I'd make a real move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the back of my head. It's like knowing the landlord might sell one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if it's still coming in five years'. Do you doubt it will happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I doubt most things that are ten years away. They promised us new radios for six years. I'll believe it when I see it, but I'm not daft, I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in my own station. If they put an AI on the front desk at Northgate and people actually used it, I'd start the course that month. Until then, I'll walk the beat.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so nobody should panic.
Probationers should **keep their notebooks**, because it might not happen.
think: At **37 and 40**, the change doesn't feel like it's about her yet.
She might be a **sergeant** or in different work by then.
do: **Carry on** with the beat and the savings as now.
Consider a **safeguarding or first aid** course in a few years.
Make a real move only if it's **still coming** in five years.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of her mind, like a **landlord** who might sell.
S4.quote: If they put an AI on the front desk at Northgate and people actually used it, I'd start the course that month.
fieldNote: She needs to **see it** in her **station** before she acts.
Promises like **new radios** that never came make her doubt long timelines.
Long time removes the urgency but not a **background worry**.

steps.text: Keep walking the Northgate beat and saving as now
Watch for AI on the Northgate front desk before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'm slow to change and that one gives nobody time, least of all me. What would help is the force paying for proper training in work time, taught by a person, not a video. And somebody promising that neighbourhood officers stay, because people in Northgate need a face they know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people on my beat. If the officers go, who knocks on Mr Haddad's door when he hasn't picked up his paper for two days? That's not something you can put in a computer.

headlineQuote: Every new system goes wrong at the start, and it's the public who pay for it.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old neighbourhood officer** in Northgate who walks the same beat and knows shopkeepers by name.
She **has never used AI**, keeps a paper notebook, and distrusts anything she can't check in court.
Her steadiest worry is **budget cuts** to her team, which has shrunk from six to four.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious and frugal**; ten years lets her mostly carry on.
She admits she tends to **wait too long**, and would only act on what she sees in her station.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she's slow to change and it gives no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Training in work time** taught by a person, not a video.
A promise that **neighbourhood officers stay** in places like Northgate.
